\section{Chapter 1}

\subsection{Example 1}

**Proposition.**
The number of partitions of $n$ in which each part appears two, three, or five times
equals the number of partitions of $n$ into parts congruent to 2, 3, 6, 9 or 10 modulo 12.

**Lemma 1.** A positive integer is congruent to 2, 3, 6, 9 or 10 modulo 12 iff it is an odd
multiple of 2 or an odd multiple of 3.

*Proof of Lemma 1.* The odd residue classes modulo 12 are [1], [3], [5], [7], [9], and [11].
An odd multiple of 2 has the form $2m$, where $m$ is odd. Thus the possible residue classes of $2m$
are
\begin{align*}
&2[1] = 2[7] = [2], \\
&2[3] = 2[9] = [6], \\
&2[5]  = 2[11] = [10].
\end{align*}
An odd multiple of 3 has the form $3m$, where $m$ is odd. Thus the possible residue classes of $3m$
are
\begin{align*}
&3[1] = 3[5] = 3[9] = [3], \\
&3[3] = 3[7] = 3[11] = [9].
\end{align*}
Therefore, the odd multiples of 2 or 3 are exactly the integers congruent to 2, 3, 6, 9, or 10
modulo 12. \hfill$\blacksquare$

*Proof of the Proposition.*
Let $p_α(n)$ denote the number of partitions of $n$
  in which each part appears two, three, or five times.
Let $p_β(n)$ denote the number of partitions of $n$
  into parts congruent to 2, 3, 6, 9, or 10 modulo 12.
Thus
$$
\sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n=\prod_{n\ge 1}\left(1+q^{2n}+q^{3n}+q^{5n}\right),
$$
and by Lemma 1
$$
\sum_{n\ge 0}p_β(n)q^n = \prod_{n\ge 1}\frac{1}{(1-q^{2(2n-1)})(1-q^{3(2n-1)})}.
$$
Finally
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{n\ge 0}p_β(n)q^n &=\prod_{n\ge 1} \frac{1-q^{4n}}{1-q^{2n}}\cdot\frac{1-q^{6n}}{1-q^{3n}} \\[0.5em]
    &=\prod_{n\ge 1}\left(1+q^{2n}\right)\left(1+q^{3n}\right)\\[0.5em]
    &=\prod_{n\ge 1}\left(1+q^{2n}+q^{3n}+q^{5n}\right)\\[0.5em]
    &=\sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n.
    \tag*{\blacksquare}
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the Proposition (q-Pochhammer)]
Let $p_α(n)$ denote the number of partitions of $n$
  in which each part appears two, three, or five times.
Let $p_β(n)$ denote the number of partitions of $n$
  into parts congruent to 2, 3, 6, 9, or 10 modulo 12.
Thus
$$
\sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n=(-q^2;q^2)_\infty (-q^3;q^3)_\infty,
$$
and by Lemma 1
$$
\sum_{n\ge 0}p_β(n)q^n = \frac{1}{(q^2;q^4)_\infty(q^3;q^6)_\infty}.
$$
Finally
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{n\ge 0}p_β(n)q^n &= \frac{(q^4;q^4)_\infty (q^6;q^6)_\infty}{(q^2;q^2)_\infty (q^3;q^3)_\infty} \\[0.5em]
      &= (-q^2;q^2)_\infty (-q^3;q^3)_\infty \\[0.5em]
      &= \sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n.
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}

\subsection{Example 2}

**Proposition.** The number of partitions of $n$ in which only odd parts may be repeated, here denoted $p_o(n)$,
equals the number of partitions of $n$ in which no part is repeated more than three times,
here denoted $p_3(n)$.

*Proof.*
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{n\ge 0} p_o(n)q^n&=\prod_{n\ge 1}\left(1+q^{2n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1-q^{2n-1}}\right)\\[0.5em]
  &=\prod_{n\ge 1}\left(\frac{1-q^{4n}}{1-q^{2n}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1-q^{2n-1}}\right)\\[0.5em]
  &=\frac{\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^{4n})}{\prod_{n\ge 1}(1-q^{2n})(1-q^{2n-1})}\\[0.5em]
  &=\prod_{n\ge 1}\frac{1-q^{4n}}{1-q^n}\\[0.5em]
  &=\sum_{n\ge 0}p_3(n)q^n.\tag*{\blacksquare}
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}[Proof (q-Pochhammer)]
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{n\ge 0} p_o(n)q^n &= (-q^2;q^2)_\infty (q;q^2)_\infty^{-1} \\
      &= \frac{(q^4;q^4)_\infty}{(q^2;q^2)_\infty (q;q^2)_\infty} \\[0.75em]
      &= \frac{(q^4;q^4)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty} \\[0.75em]
      &= \sum_{n\ge 0} p_3(n)q^n.
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}

\newpage
\subsection{Example 3}

**Proposition.** The number of partitions of $n$ in which only parts $\not\equiv0(\bmod\, 2^m)$ may
be repeated, here denoted $p_α(n)$, equals the number of partitions of $n$ in which no part appears
more than $2^{m+1}-1$ times, here denoted $p_β(n)$.

*Proof.*
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n &= \prod_{n\ge 1}\left(1+q^{2^mn}\right)\left(\frac{1-q^{2^mn}}{1-q^n}\right)\\[0.5em]
    &= \prod_{n\ge 1} \left(1+q^{2^mn}\right) \left(1+q^n+\cdots+q^{(2^m-1)n}\right)\\[0.5em]
    &= \prod_{n\ge 1} \left(1+q^n+\cdots+q^{(2^{m+1}-1)n}\right)\\[0.5em]
    &= \prod_{n\ge 1} \frac{1-q^{2^{m+1}n}}{1-q^n}\\[0.5em]
    &= \sum_{n\ge 0} p_β(n)q^n.
    \tag*{\blacksquare}
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}[Proof (q-Pochhammer)]
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{n\ge 0}p_α(n)q^n &= (-q^{2^m},q^{2^m};q^{2^m})_\infty (q;q)_\infty^{-1} \\
      &= \frac{(q^{2^{m+1}};q^{2^{m+1}})_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty} \\[0.75em]
      &= \sum_{n\ge 0} p_β(n)q^n.
  \end{align*}
\end{proof}
